doc.title: Mike Davis interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 1, 2024

title: The transcription and play-along project with Cole
summary: Davis describes the new twelve-standards series with Mike Rodriguez and Marshall Gilkes and the value of transcribing solos like Freddie Hubbard's.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What’s on your plate at the moment that you’re working on?

I’m actually working on a new series of — what do I want to call them — it’s twelve standards, two choruses on each standard, and my son and I, Cole and I, are producing it together. We’re getting some of our favorite brass players so we’re starting with Mike Rodriguez and Marshall Gilkes. They — we send them the rhythm tracks which Cole sort of organized, and then we’re transcribing all their solos and putting it out as a transcription book, also you’ll get the play-along tracks that you can play yourself along with an analysis of what they’re actually — how they’re approaching various chords and whatnot. And it’s all standards. It’s everything from “All The Things You Are” to “Giant Steps” to “Bolivia” to “Stella By Starlight,” you know things like that and “Impressions.” So that’s a really time consuming project. I didn’t think it was going to be this time consuming. I’m trying to get Mike’s — we’re starting with Mike Rodriguez’s book and I’m down to my — in fact as soon as we finish today I’m going to have to finish up the last solo but I’m close to finishing it. But I wish he wasn’t quite as good as he is but that’s just what it is.
“It’s too hard to transcribe you, man.”

And sometimes I’ve read reviews and, in DownBeat, dissecting solos and trying to make sense of what someone’s doing over a certain chord symbol and the lengths that you may have to go to to say okay they’re playing the sharp nine here and they played it two bars before that. And I guess what I’m trying to say, sometimes it’s hard to explain why people do things.

Yeah, totally. And I think the most valuable thing is not — I mean it’s valuable to have an analysis of it for sure. But to me the most valuable thing is seeing — I mean I’ve worn out my Freddie Hubbard book that I think Hal Leonard might be the publisher of it. I mean those became like the same as the classical etudes that I would practice every day and like we called it they’re “Rochut Etudes” — these vocal etudes that are very, very standard in the trombone pedagogue world. But the Freddie Hubbard solos to me are just as important and just as applicable. So you know really trying to mirror his phrasing, that’s the real import of this project I think. But having an analysis makes it — pardon me — having the analysis certainly makes it — if you want to dive into that it gives you that option to do that.
